newsitem.title: CHINA: Tung says HK life goes on as usual after handover.
newsitem.headline: Tung says HK life goes on as usual after handover.

text.p: Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa celebrated the capitalist territory's first month as part of China on Thursday, claiming that life had not changed at all.
Tung said the first month under Chinese rule showed Hong Kong had remained a free market economy, where the rule of law reigned and people were free to express their political views.
"If people ask me what has been the biggest change since July 1, I would say there has been no big change. It is business as usual," Tung told the Australian Chamber of Commerce.
Hong Kong reverted to Beijing's control on July 1 after 156 years of British colonial rule, and became a highly autonomous Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China.
Tung said that in the 31 days since the change of flag Hong Kong people had kept their rights and freedoms as guaranteed by the new constitution, the Basic Law.
"There are demonstrations as usual, lawsuits as usual, media scrutiny as usual," Tung said. "Indeed, this is part of our culture and it would be unusual if this were not the case."
This week a Hong Kong appeal court crushed a challenge to the legality of the unelected Provisional Legislature installed by Beijing, averting a potential constitutional crisis.
Tung said some of his friends had asked him if he was disappointed that the Provisional Legislature was challenged in the first month after the handover.
"The answer is no, because it shows to the people of Hong Kong and to those in the rest of the world that the rule of law is of paramount importance to Hong Kong," he said.
The rule of law must be preserved by all means, he said.
"All that I do, all that the government does, must be in accordance with the law because the rule of law is essential for the continued success of Hong Kong."
Tung said he expected the courts would soon hear another case challenging the system, when it considers the plight of mainland-born children facing deportation from Hong Kong.
Tung, formally known as Chief Executive, has repeatedly said "livelihood issues" are most important to Hong Kong people rather than political rights and democracy.
He said his government was committed to providing a "decent life" for those who cannot help themselves and the necessary training for people that can.
He defended the legislature's freezing of pre-handover labour rights laws, saying they were pushed through without due consideration and threatened Hong Kong's competitive edge.

"I am sure that after careful consideration and consultation with all sides, we will be able to find the right way forward in maintaining Hong Kong's economic vitality which in turn will mean more job opportunities for everyone," he said.
Tung also touched upon another issue of immense importance to Hong Kong people as well as to investors in the territory's booming stock market -- the outlook for the property sector.

He reiterated his belief that increasing housing supply was the best way to dampen speculation and cool red hot property prices, adding that the government had the will and the means to meet its targets for building new homes.
He promised a "level playing field" for foreign business, but declined to speculate on corporate tax cuts which are now demanded by some legislators and by business lobbies.
